titleEn: European Research Aims to Use Sensors to Manage Fertilizer Waste
titleZh: 欧洲研究拟用传感器管理肥料浪费
summaryZh: 丹麦与德国合作开展NutriCycle项目，开发基于微流控和光学传感器的自动化系统，可实时测量温室水中各营养物浓度，帮助种植者精准补充缺失养分而非丢弃整池水肥，从而节约成本并减少氮磷进入废水。项目为期三年，将在德国温室进行原型测试，并计划接入现有数字平台实现自动化控制。
featuredReason: 该新闻展示了传感器与微流控技术在设施园艺中的精准水肥管理应用，对智慧畜牧行业从事温室环境控制、自动化灌溉和废弃物资源化的读者具有直接参考价值。
contentFull:
By Greenhouse Grower staff|September 24, 2026 

 

 

 

 In a modern greenhouse, water draining from beneath the plants is often collected, filtered, treated with UV light, and returned to the plants with a mixture of nutrients, including nitrate, phosphate and magnesium.

 Even so, greenhouses periodically discard the water and start again with a fresh mixture. The problem is that existing measurements typically show only the total concentration of dissolved salts in the water. They do not reveal which nutrients are present in excess and which are running low. As a result, water that still contains usable and costly fertilizer may be sent down the drain.

 Researchers from the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) and Kiel University hope to change that through a new Danish–German project: NutriCycle. Working with the horticulture industry and Danish water utility VandCenter Syd, they plan to develop an automated sensor system that can measure individual nutrients in greenhouse water.

 “Plants take up different nutrients depending on factors such as their variety and stage of growth. Today, growers can see the overall salt concentration in the water, but not exactly what is missing,” says Casper Kunstmann of the Mads Clausen Institute at SDU, who leads the project. “If we can measure the individual nutrients, they could add, for example, phosphate or nitrate instead of discarding the entire mixture.”

 A Miniature Laboratory for the Greenhouse

 The researchers will develop a compact device that automatically takes and analyses small water samples. SDU will contribute its expertise in microfluidics, which makes it possible to move and examine tiny amounts of liquid on a chip.

 Inside the system, small droplets of water will undergo chemical reactions that change their color according to what they contain. Optical sensors developed by Kiel University will then read the colors to determine the concentration of each nutrient.

 The aim is to bring these steps together in a robust, relatively inexpensive device that can be connected to existing greenhouse irrigation systems.

 “Equipment that can measure the different nutrients already exists, but integrating it can be costly. We want to develop a smaller, more efficient solution from the ground up that is also simple enough to use in the day-to-day running of a greenhouse,” Kunstmann says.

 The plan is to connect the system to the digital platform InfoGrow, which is already used to monitor and control greenhouse conditions, including temperature, heating, windows and screens. In time, nutrient levels in the water could become part of the same automated control system.

 Casper Kunstmann of the Mads Clausen Institute at SDU

 Benefits for Growers and the Environment

 More precise control could help growers save both water and fertilizer. Unlike crops grown in fields, greenhouse plants are typically supplied with mineral nutrients added directly to the water. That makes it costly to discard a mixture that still contains nutrients.

 “The green transition also has to make economic sense for growers. If they can keep water circulating for longer and add only the nutrients the plants actually need, they can save resources and reduce their costs,” Kunstmann says.

 The technology could also reduce the amount of nutrients entering wastewater. Excessive amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus can contribute to algal growth and oxygen depletion if they reach rivers, lakes or coastal waters.

 This is one reason why VandCenter Syd is taking part in the project. The company will help test the technology for use in wastewater treatment. In the longer term, the partners hope the system could also monitor treated wastewater and help make it possible to reuse more water in agriculture.

 Testing in a German Greenhouse

 The three-year project is led by the Mads Clausen Institute at SDU. The other partners are Kiel University, VandCenter Syd, the Danish horticultural consultancy HortiAdvice, and the German plant breeding and horticultural company NPZ Innovation.

 In the first phase, the researchers will establish how much water and fertilizer is currently lost and develop the measurement method. They will then assemble the technology in a prototype and test it under real conditions at NPZ Innovation in Germany.

 “The crucial thing is to develop something that works in a laboratory and can also withstand everyday life in a greenhouse. Growers need to be able to rely on the system without it creating a lot of extra work,” Kunstmann says.

translationZh:
在现代温室中，从植物下方排出的水通常会被收集、过滤、用紫外线处理，然后与包括硝酸盐、磷酸盐和镁在内的营养物混合后返回给植物。

即便如此，温室仍会定期丢弃这些水并重新配制新混合液。问题在于，现有测量通常只能显示水中溶解盐的总浓度，无法揭示哪些营养物过剩、哪些即将耗尽。结果，仍含有可用且昂贵肥料的水可能被直接排入下水道。

南丹麦大学和基尔大学的研究人员希望通过一个新的丹麦-德国项目NutriCycle来改变这一现状。他们计划与园艺行业及丹麦水务公司VandCenter Syd合作，开发一种能够测量温室水中各单一营养物的自动化传感器系统。

“植物会根据品种和生长阶段等因素吸收不同的营养物。如今种植者可以看到水中的总盐浓度，但无法确切知道缺少什么，”该项目负责人、南丹麦大学Mads Clausen研究所的Casper Kunstmann说。“如果我们能测量各单一营养物，他们就可以例如添加磷酸盐或硝酸盐，而不是丢弃整个混合液。”

**温室中的微型实验室**

研究人员将开发一种紧凑设备，可自动采集并分析少量水样。南丹麦大学将贡献其在微流控方面的专业知识，使在芯片上移动和检测微量液体成为可能。

在系统内部，小水滴将发生化学反应，根据其含量改变颜色。基尔大学开发的光学传感器随后读取颜色，以确定每种营养物的浓度。

目标是将这些步骤整合到一个坚固、相对廉价的设备中，并可连接到现有的温室灌溉系统。

“能够测量不同营养物的设备已经存在，但集成成本可能很高。我们希望从头开发一种更小、更高效的解决方案，同时足够简单，便于温室日常运行中使用，”Kunstmann说。

计划是将该系统连接到数字平台InfoGrow，该平台已用于监测和控制温室条件，包括温度、供暖、窗户和遮阳幕。随着时间的推移，水中的营养物水平可能成为同一自动化控制系统的一部分。

**为种植者和环境带来益处**

更精准的控制可以帮助种植者节约水和肥料。与田间作物不同，温室植物通常通过直接添加到水中的矿物营养物来供给。这使得丢弃仍含营养物的混合液成本高昂。

“绿色转型也必须对种植者具有经济意义。如果他们能让水循环使用更长时间，并且只添加植物实际需要的营养物，就能节约资源并降低成本，”Kunstmann说。

该技术还可以减少进入废水的营养物数量。过量的氮和磷如果进入河流、湖泊或沿海水域，可能导致藻类生长和氧气耗尽。

这是VandCenter Syd参与该项目的原因之一。该公司将帮助测试该技术在废水处理中的应用。从长远来看，合作伙伴希望该系统还能监测处理后的废水，并帮助实现农业中更多水的再利用。

**在德国温室中进行测试**

这个为期三年的项目由南丹麦大学Mads Clausen研究所牵头。其他合作伙伴包括基尔大学、VandCenter Syd、丹麦园艺咨询公司HortiAdvice，以及德国植物育种和园艺公司NPZ Innovation。

在第一阶段，研究人员将确定目前损失了多少水和肥料，并开发测量方法。随后，他们将把技术组装成原型，并在德国NPZ Innovation的真实条件下进行测试。

“关键是要开发出既能在实验室工作，又能承受温室日常生活的东西。种植者需要能够依赖该系统，而不会因此产生大量额外工作，”Kunstmann说。
author: Brian Sparks
contentHtml:
Researchers in Denmark and Germany plan to develop an automated sensor system that can measure individual nutrients in greenhouse water.
The post European Research Aims to Use Sensors to Manage Fertilizer Waste appeared first on Greenhouse Grower.
